new_statements.quote: Stress is generally predictable, with primary stress on the penultimate syllable of the word, and secondary stress on every second syllable preceding. [...] Words that originated in Proto Oceanic with a final consonant have had an echo vowel added in Mussau, but the stress remains on the penultimate syllable of the underlying form, and thus on the antepenultimate syllable of the modern form. The other exception is that stress can be shifted towards the beginning of the word when a stress vowel is immediately preceded by an identical or lower vowel (which we are analysing as a diphthong), or preceded by an /a/ with a consonant intervening.

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog record (StressTyp2 penultimate stress = penultimate). Adds: alternating secondary stress leftward, stress recomputed over suffixes and clitics, and two exception classes (historical echo-vowel words with antepenult stress; optional leftward shift near diphthongs / preceding /a/).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress on the penultimate syllable of the word; secondary stress on every second syllable to the left of the primary (alternating trochaic pattern). Stress is recomputed to the penult when suffixes or clitics are added (p. 5: 'Stress shifts to the penultimate vowel with the addition of suffixes and clitics').
new_statements.secondary_stress: 'secondary stress on every second syllable preceding' the penultimate primary stress (p. 4).
new_statements.exceptions: (1) Words that had a final consonant in Proto-Oceanic and acquired an echo vowel keep stress on the historical penult, i.e. the antepenult of the modern form (examples p. 5: *padran > 'arana 'pandanus', *panas > 'aanasa 'hot', *pulan > 'ulana 'moon'). (2) Optional leftward shift when the stressed vowel is immediately preceded by an identical or lower vowel (analysed as a diphthong) or by /a/ with a consonant between; 'this latter exception is optional, with examples of stress in both positions being observed' (p. 5). Attributed to Malcolm Ross's analysis.
new_statements.identity_note: The OPD describes 'Mussau-Emira Language, St Matthias Islands, New Ireland Province', with data from the Mussau villages Lomakunauru, Palakau, Nae, Tasitel, Loverang, Lolieng, Katulusae, Magean and Loaua; this is the same language as Glottolog muss1246 (Mussau-Emira), no separate dialect singled out.

audit.recode_to: fixed-dominant penultimate (not in the strict set; domain = penultimate mora/vowel, final long vowel stressed; the exceptions statement = lexical antepenultimate class + optional retraction) - or 'weight' with what counts as heavy: CVV (final long vowel attracts stress) if the catalog treats this pattern as it does for Samoan/Tongan
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: confirmed verbatim in the ANU PDF we hold of Blust 1984 at p.173 (secs 2.4.2-2.4.3), paragraph running to p.174. (2) Deciding source: Blust 1984 is a vocabulary with phonological notes (primary fieldwork, competent, open), reached via StressTyp2/Gordon 2002. It is not the last word: Blust 2001 (OL 40) is a dedicated stress article and Ross 2002 / Brownie & Brownie 2007 are later descriptions; the 2007 grammar and 2002 OPD are. (3) What the held later sources say, and why the classification is at risk: the record is classification fixed-strict, counts as exceptionless (the strict set), rule = penultimate syllable. (a) Blust 1984 itself (same p.173) states the regularity over the penultimate MORA because vowel length is contrastive and a final long vowel carries stress ([bao] 'carry pick-a-back' vs [bao:] 'rain'); the catalog codes this same 'last vowel if long, else penult' pattern as 'weight' (CVV) for Samoan and T
audit.second_reader_evidence: The quotation was checked again:, confirmed. lines 798-846 = PL A-69 p.173 (running head 'A MUSSAU VOCABULARY, WITH PHONOLOGICAL NOTES 173') sec. 2.4.2 'In the great majority of cases primary stress was recorded on the penultimate vocoid: [rame] chew, [sesa] one, [aroa] cuscus, [taliŋa] ear, [malataw] flesh, meat, [ramuramutipa] tongue'; same page 'primary stress can be assigned to the penultimate mora of the word'; sec. 2.4.3 'stress shifts after affixation so as to remain on the penultimate syllabic of the word: /nima/.. /nima-gi/.. /niu/ [niw].. /niu-na/ [niyúna]', paragraph running onto p.174 ('174 ROBERT BLUST'). Locator pp.173-174 secs 2.
